title: Rise of Churches Aligned With Zionism Made Chiapas an Israel-Friendly Zone
author: Hermann Bellinghausen
content:
_This article by[Hermann
Bellinghausen](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Hermann%20Bellinghausen,%20enviado)
originally appeared in the [October 26, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/26/politica/auge-de-
iglesias-afines-al-sionismo-hizo-a-chiapas-zona-israel-friendly), Mexico's
premier left wing daily newspaper._

**San Cristóbal de Las Casas, Chiapas**. Chiapas stands out for experiencing
religious events of diverse kinds with important political implications, and
not only social ones. The variety and dispersion of churches and Christian
denominations is impressive in a state with a large number of formally
established religious or mystical expressions. For decades, San Cristóbal de
Las Casas has been the epicenter of a plurality of beliefs perhaps unique in
Mexico.

In recent years the activity of Zionist Christian churches has become
noticeable; in the face of the genocide perpetrated by Israel in Gaza for
three years, **they choose to back it** , something very similar to what has
transformed the political-religious map of Latin America, which has become
**the only Israel _friendly_ area in the world outside Europe and the white
extensions of the British empire**.

So dynamic are the churches and religious affiliations in Chiapas,
particularly in Los Altos, that even the Catholic Church, the oldest,
experienced differences when the so-called Liberation Theology was established
here under the leadership and inspiration of Bishop Samuel Ruiz García, with
an open preference for the Maya Indigenous peoples, above all starting with
the historic National Indigenous Congress of 1974 in San Andrés Larráinzar.

Its success brought it into confrontation with the conservative Catholicism of
the dominant classes and with the PRI State, until reaching the climax with
the Indigenous insurrection of 1994. Although the Zapatista Army of National
Liberation (EZLN) has always avoided any religious identity and opts for the
peoples' freedom of belief, it is known that its civilian bases and allied
organizations in the jungle, the north and Los Altos are mostly liberationist
Catholics.

![Ceremony in San Cristóbal de Las Casas during the signing of the Unity Pact
of religious associations](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/chiapas-israel-friendly-02-pacto-unidad.jpg)Ceremony
in San Cristóbal de Las Casas, on March 19, 2005, during the signing of the
Unity Pact of religious associations. Photo: Víctor Camacho

As indisputable as they are difficult to document, the “traditional” or
syncretic beliefs, perhaps with pre-Hispanic elements, form part of the deep
religiosity of these communities that already lived here before the sword and
the Cross.

San Cristóbal de las Casas was already a peculiarly cosmopolitan place before
the galloping gentrification of the Pueblos Mágicos. As for religion, Buddhist
and Eastern meditation centers abound, two Islamic mosques with a
fundamentally Tsotsil base operate, decades ago a Sikh community was
established here and more recently a discreet Hasidic colony that practices
Orthodox Judaism. But if anything changed the social and religious profile of
the municipality and the city of San Cristóbal it was the mass expulsion of
families from neighboring San Juan Chamula, who left “traditional Catholicism”
in the 1980s and joined evangelical and Pentecostal churches, only to be
violently persecuted by the political-religious power of the Chamula town
council.

Established in the Jovel valley and in other parts of San Cristóbal, they
founded numerous neighborhoods and settlements, today heavily populated and
bustling. The dominant note is the countless temples one finds, of a great
number of denominations, some as powerful as the Jehovah's Witnesses, others
Pentecostal, or Tsotsil churches, above all to the north and west of the city.
The same in new urban centers such as Betania. Some evangelical variants such
as La Roca and El Guardián de mi Hermano have carried out actions of a
military type, generally non-violent, although the former has been associated
with the gang _Los Motonetos_. As a whole, the Chamula exile in San Cristóbal
constitutes a political, economic and religious power.

It should not be overlooked that the paramilitary groups of the 1990s were
made up of evangelicals, and their victims were Zapatista bases or those of
allied Catholic organizations in the Chol and Tsotsil regions, as could be
seen with the Acteal massacre against Las Abejas in 1997 and the massacres in
the northern zone.

Against this backdrop, some denominations veered toward a Christian Zionism
very similar to what has occurred in Central America, the entire Andean region
and the Amazonian territories of seven countries, where the spread of
Protestant churches has been continuous for decades. From there it is only one
step to explicit or tacit support for the State of Israel. Thus, they have
become the gateway for Israeli expansionism through religious practices that
are less and less Christian and that lead to a sort of second-tier Judaism,
encouraged by similar churches from the United States that for decades have
practiced a religious colonialism with profound consequences for the community
life of the original peoples of Chiapas.

Benjamin Netanyahu already expressed it during a visit to Brazil in 2019:

> We have no better friends in the world than the evangelical community, and
> the evangelical community has no better friend in the world than the State
> of Israel.
>
> Benjamin Netanyahu, Brazil, 2019

There are 600 million believers, 133 in Latin America, of whom there would be
10 in Mexico. In Brazil there are close to 50 million, and in the United
States more than 90.

The association of non-Catholic churches and Christian organizations with
Judaism is not new. What is new is the pro-Israeli turn that pastors and
“friends” of their churches have surreptitiously induced. Norman Lewis, the
writer and chronicler who gave rise to Survival International, warned for
years about the effects of these new missions, which promote individualism and
what is today called the “prosperity theology,” which goes directly against
the solidarity-based, participatory and communal culture of the Indigenous
peoples of the continent.

He observed this in South America, Central America, Mexico, even on other
continents. In 1983 he pointed out that the “born-again” fundamentalist
missionaries, recruited in the United States for the New Tribes Mission “with
impressive technical equipment and abundant funds,” announced the “second
coming of Jesus Christ,” the end of the world and the salvation of the true
believers.

Over time, many subordinated themselves to Judaism in the official version of
the State of Israel, and consequently support Israeli military actions in
Palestine and Lebanon. Paradoxically, they could be described as more
“religious” than the Israeli State, more military than theocratic, where
“democratic” selectivity prevented for 70 years the full inclusion of Islamic
or Christian Palestinians; political participation was always the privilege of
the Jewish minority. In another paradox, evangelical fervor, in its
unconditional devotion to the mythical and the real Israel, finds little
appreciation in Israel, where the population treats them as intruders and
there is no shortage of those who spit as they pass; they do not consider them
their equals.

A notable expression of this syncretism is the Church of God of New Testament
Judaism, a religious congregation that expressly mixes the Christian faith of
the New Testament with practices and elements of biblical Judaism, to the
point of centering on salvation, perfection and sanctification through the
study and practice of biblical Judaism, and sharing with it the wait for the
Messiah, the return of Yeshua Ha-Mashiach. It is headed in Mexico and Latin
America by the apostle Tito Galván Zafra. Its action groups are: Sons of
Abraham, Ladies of Ruth, The Valiant of David and Here I Am. It has a presence
in various states of the center and south of the country, but in Chiapas they
have drawn attention for their closeness to the Israeli missions of **young
members of the Israel Defense Forces, who take part, particularly from Tuxtla
Gutiérrez and San Cristóbal de Las Casas, in “solidarity” incursions into
Indigenous schools** in Zinacantán, Chamula, Oxchuc and San Cristóbal itself.
